subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: An 18-year-old man has a family history of colorectal cancer. Colonoscopy reveals hundreds of polyps throughout the colon, including the rectum, that began appearing after puberty. Genetic testing shows a germline mutation in a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 5q21-q22.
question: Which of the following best describes this disorder?

options.text: Autosomal recessive MUTYH mutation with duodenal and ovarian cancers
Autosomal dominant APC mutation; without prophylactic colectomy, progression to CRC is essentially 100%
Autosomal dominant mismatch repair mutation with approximately 80% CRC risk
Autosomal dominant hamartomatous polyps with mucocutaneous pigmentation
An autosomal dominant syndrome with osteomas and CHRPE but a normal APC gene

explanation_correct: Familial adenomatous polyposis is autosomal dominant from a mutation in the APC tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 5q21-q22, following the two-hit hypothesis. Thousands of polyps arise starting after puberty, are pancolonic, and always involve the rectum. Without prophylactic colectomy, essentially 100% of patients progress to colorectal cancer.

explanation_incorrect.A: MUTYH-associated polyposis is autosomal recessive, involves a DNA repair gene, and is associated with duodenal adenomas and ovarian/bladder cancers, not APC on chromosome 5q.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lynch syndrome is autosomal dominant from mismatch repair gene mutations (MLH1/MSH2) with about 80% CRC risk and proximal colon involvement, not thousands of polyps.
explanation_incorrect.D: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome features hamartomatous polyps and hyperpigmented macules, not APC-mutated adenomatous polyps.
explanation_incorrect.E: Gardner syndrome is FAP plus osteomas, CHRPE, and dental anomalies; it still results from an APC mutation rather than a normal APC gene.

educationalObjective: FAP is an AD APC (5q21-q22) polyposis syndrome with thousands of polyps after puberty, rectal involvement, and near-100% CRC risk without colectomy.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 22-year-old man with familial adenomatous polyposis also has osteomas of the mandible, impacted teeth, and congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium.
question: Which syndrome does this combination describe?
explanation_correct: Gardner syndrome is familial adenomatous polyposis plus osseous and soft tissue tumors (eg, osteomas of the skull or mandible), congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE), and impacted or supernumerary teeth. The underlying defect is still an APC mutation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Turcot syndrome is FAP or Lynch syndrome plus a malignant CNS tumor such as medulloblastoma or glioma, not osteomas and CHRPE.
explanation_incorrect.B: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome features hamartomatous polyps and hyperpigmented macules on the mouth, lips, hands, and genitalia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Juvenile polyposis is a childhood autosomal dominant hamartomatous syndrome, not associated with osteomas or CHRPE.
explanation_incorrect.E: Lynch syndrome is a mismatch repair disorder with proximal colorectal cancer and endometrial, ovarian, and skin cancers, without these FAP stigmata.

educationalObjective: Gardner syndrome equals FAP plus osteomas/soft tissue tumors, CHRPE, and impacted or supernumerary teeth.
source: Generated from 9. Gastrointestinal.pdf - Pathology: Polyposis syndromes

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 42-year-old woman with multiple adenomatous and serrated colonic polyps and early-onset colorectal cancer has a pedigree in which unaffected parents are carriers and several siblings are affected. Genetic testing shows a defect in a gene responsible for DNA repair.
question: Which of the following is most likely?

options.text: Autosomal recessive MUTYH-associated polyposis with duodenal, ovarian, and bladder cancer risk
Autosomal dominant FAP with 100% CRC risk without colectomy
Autosomal dominant Lynch syndrome with endometrial cancer
Autosomal dominant Peutz-Jeghers syndrome with mucocutaneous pigmentation
Juvenile polyposis syndrome presenting for the first time in adulthood

explanation_correct: MUTYH-associated polyposis is an autosomal recessive disorder of the MUTYH gene responsible for DNA repair. It markedly increases the risk of colorectal cancer and polyps (adenomatous, and may be hyperplastic or serrated) and serrated adenomas. It is also associated with duodenal adenomas and ovarian and bladder cancers. The affected-siblings-with-carrier-parents pedigree fits recessive inheritance.

explanation_incorrect.B: FAP is autosomal dominant from an APC mutation with near-100% CRC risk and no ovarian/bladder association; the pedigree here is recessive.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant mismatch repair disorder with proximal colon and endometrial/ovarian/skin cancers, not a recessive DNA repair gene defect.
explanation_incorrect.D: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is autosomal dominant with hamartomas and hyperpigmented macules, not a MUTYH DNA repair defect.
explanation_incorrect.E: Juvenile polyposis typically presents in children under 5 years with hamartomas, not DNA-repair-associated serrated adenomas in a 42-year-old.

educationalObjective: MUTYH-associated polyposis is an AR DNA-repair polyposis syndrome with adenomatous/serrated polyps and duodenal, ovarian, and bladder cancer risk.
source: Generated from 9. Gastrointestinal.pdf - Pathology: Polyposis syndromes

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 15-year-old with a polyposis syndrome develops a malignant brain tumor. Pathology shows a medulloblastoma. Genetic workup reveals a mutation consistent with either familial adenomatous polyposis or Lynch syndrome.
question: Which syndrome is characterized by intestinal polyposis plus a malignant CNS tumor?
explanation_correct: Turcot syndrome is familial adenomatous polyposis or Lynch syndrome plus a malignant CNS tumor such as medulloblastoma or glioma. The mnemonic is Turcot equals Turban, linking the syndrome to a brain tumor. This patient's medulloblastoma in the setting of polyposis fits the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Gardner syndrome is FAP plus osteomas, soft tissue tumors, CHRPE, and dental anomalies, not malignant CNS tumors.
explanation_incorrect.B: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome features hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation, not malignant CNS tumors.
explanation_incorrect.C: Juvenile polyposis is a childhood hamartomatous syndrome without associated CNS tumors.
explanation_incorrect.D: MUTYH-associated polyposis is AR with adenomatous/serrated polyps and duodenal, ovarian, and bladder cancers, not CNS tumors.

educationalObjective: Turcot syndrome equals FAP or Lynch syndrome plus a malignant CNS tumor (medulloblastoma or glioma).
source: Generated from 9. Gastrointestinal.pdf - Pathology: Polyposis syndromes

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 19-year-old woman has numerous hamartomatous polyps throughout the GI tract and dark hyperpigmented macules on her lips, mouth, hands, and genitalia.
question: Which syndrome is this?
explanation_correct: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is autosomal dominant, featuring numerous hamartomatous polyps throughout the GI tract along with hyperpigmented macules on the mouth, lips, hands, and genitalia. It is associated with an increased risk of breast and GI cancers, including colorectal, stomach, small bowel, and pancreatic cancer.

explanation_incorrect.A: Juvenile polyposis has hamartomatous polyps in young children but lacks the characteristic mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation.
explanation_incorrect.B: Gardner syndrome is FAP with osteomas, CHRPE, and dental anomalies, not hyperpigmented macules.
explanation_incorrect.D: Turcot syndrome is FAP or Lynch syndrome plus a malignant CNS tumor, not hamartomas with pigmentation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Lynch syndrome is a mismatch repair disorder with proximal colorectal and endometrial, ovarian, and skin cancers, not hamartomas or mucocutaneous pigmentation.

educationalObjective: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is AD hamartomatous GI polyps plus hyperpigmented macules on lips, mouth, hands, and genitalia with increased breast and GI cancer risk.
